Rain: use wet or intermediate tyres, brake earlier and keep the inputs smooth. Kerbs and painted lines have almost no grip.
Damp track: the racing line dries first. Avoid kerbs and keep the tyres on the dry line.
Hot track: tyres overheat quickly, the rears first. Soft tyres degrade faster; manage wheelspin on exits.
Cold track: tyres need longer to reach their window. Expect less grip on the first laps and after a pit stop.
The track is heating up: grip drops a little and tyre wear grows. Lap times may drift up.
The track is cooling down: grip improves, but tyres may fall below their window on long straights.
Strong wind: braking points move with a headwind or tailwind, and fast corners feel different lap to lap.
Stable, dry conditions: nothing changes the plan.

Balance compares how much you steer with how much the car actually turns (lateral G and speed). Locking and wheelspin come from wheel speed against car speed, bottoming from the suspension resting at its lowest point at speed, tyre balance from front and rear temperatures. These are rules of thumb, not a simulation: your feel in the car wins.
The front washes wide while you brake and turn in.
At the apex the car needs more lock than the corner asks for.
On power the car runs wide: a tight differential pushes it straight.
The rear steps out under braking.
The rear lets go at the apex.
The rear slides on power and you catch it with counter-steer.
The front wheels slow down faster than the car under heavy braking.
The rear wheels lock under braking, which makes the car unstable.
The rear wheels spin faster than the car on throttle.
The front wheels spin on throttle (front or all-wheel drive).
At speed the front suspension often sits at its lowest point.
At speed the rear suspension often sits at its lowest point.
The fronts run much hotter than the rears: they slide more.
The rears run much hotter than the fronts: they slide more.

The tyres run too hot: try a harder compound and less wheelspin and sliding.
